title: Health literacy and health outcomes in patients with low back pain: a scoping review

subsections.subsection_title: Core Outcomes and Knowledge Assessment in Low Back Pain
subsections.content: The assessment of core outcomes in non-specific low back pain (NSLBP) has been standardized through the development of a consensus-based core outcome set (COS), which ensures comparability across clinical trials. The COS for NSLBP, established through an international Delphi study using the OMERACT Filter 2.0 framework, identifies essential domains including pain intensity, physical functioning, health-related quality of life, and patient global impression of change, thereby minimizing outcome reporting heterogeneity ref [1]. Beyond clinical trial outcomes, patient-reported knowledge and understanding of their condition are critical determinants of self-management and long-term outcomes. Health education literacy—defined as the capacity to comprehend, apply, and communicate health-related information—has been specifically operationalized in chronic musculoskeletal populations through the HELP questionnaire, which assesses three dimensions: comprehension of medical information, application of health advice, and communicative competence with providers ref [4]. In clinical settings, brief screening tools can efficiently identify patients with limited health literacy, such as the single-item question, 'How confident are you filling out medical forms by yourself?', which demonstrated high accuracy (AUROC = 0.82) in detecting limited or marginal literacy skills ref [7]. These tools enable targeted interventions to bridge knowledge gaps and improve health outcomes in patients with NSLBP.

This scoping review was conducted following the methodological framework initially proposed by Arksey and O'Malley, which outlines a six-stage process for identifying, selecting, and synthesizing evidence across broad research domains ref [4]. This framework was subsequently refined by Levac et al., who emphasized the importance of iterative team-based study selection, transparent data extraction, and the integration of stakeholder consultation as a mandatory knowledge translation component ref [6]. To ensure rigorous reporting and methodological transparency, we adhered to the PRISMA-ScR checklist, which provides 20 essential reporting items specifically designed for scoping reviews and enhances reproducibility and utility for policymakers and clinicians ref [5]. The review process included defining the research question, identifying relevant studies through systematic database searches, screening titles and abstracts, full-text assessment, data extraction, and thematic synthesis. Unlike systematic reviews, which aim to answer focused clinical questions, this scoping review sought to map the breadth of literature on health literacy and low back pain outcomes, identify key concepts, and highlight gaps in measurement and reporting. All stages were conducted by at least two independent reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through consensus or third-party arbitration.

The inclusion criteria were deliberately broad to capture diverse conceptualizations of health literacy and heterogeneous outcome measures in low back pain populations, aligning with the exploratory nature of scoping reviews. A consultation phase with content experts and patient advocates was incorporated to validate findings and ensure relevance to clinical and policy contexts, as recommended in recent methodological advances ref [6]. This approach not only strengthened the validity of the synthesis but also enhanced the translational potential of the review's outcomes.

Health literacy has evolved from a narrow focus on functional skills—such as reading prescription labels and appointment slips—to a multidimensional construct encompassing interactive and critical capacities. Early definitions, such as that by the Institute of Medicine, framed health literacy as the ability to obtain, process, and understand basic health information to make informed decisions ref [10]. However, Nutbeam expanded this view by proposing a three-tiered model: functional, interactive, and critical health literacy, where the latter involves the ability to critically analyze health information and advocate for structural change ref [8]. This progression underscores that health literacy is not merely an individual skill but a dynamic capacity shaped by social, cultural, and political contexts ref [9].

Measurement of health literacy has similarly diversified. Traditional tools like the Test of Functional Health Literacy in Adults (TOFHLA) and the Newest Vital Sign (NVS) assess functional and numeracy skills through standardized tasks, with the NVS gaining popularity for its brevity and applicability in primary care settings ref [7], ref [8]. More recent innovations, such as Health LiTT, leverage item response theory and touchscreen technology to provide a more nuanced, adaptive, and psychometrically robust assessment across prose, document, and quantitative domains, particularly useful in diverse and underserved populations ref [9]. These instruments reflect a shift from static, one-dimensional measures toward dynamic, context-sensitive evaluations that align with contemporary conceptualizations of health literacy as an empowering, action-oriented competency.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy and Low Back Pain Outcomes
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence suggests that health literacy significantly influences outcomes in individuals with low back pain (LBP), particularly through its impact on pain perception, self-management behaviors, and psychological factors. Studies have demonstrated that lower health literacy is associated with higher pain intensity and poorer pain management, as individuals with limited health literacy struggle to interpret and act upon clinical advice ref [16]. Furthermore, patients with chronic LBP exhibit reduced confidence in managing their condition, particularly in domains related to personal health attitudes, which may hinder engagement in recommended lifestyle modifications ref [14].

Health literacy also correlates with maladaptive cognitive patterns such as fear-avoidance beliefs, which are known predictors of disability in LBP. Research among women with chronic LBP found that lower health literacy was significantly linked to stronger fear-avoidance beliefs, suggesting that inadequate understanding of LBP mechanisms may reinforce catastrophic thinking and behavioral avoidance ref [6]. Similarly, a mixed-methods study revealed that individuals with CLBP held more negative beliefs about the inevitability and severity of pain, which were associated with lower health literacy scores ref [13].

The development of condition-specific knowledge tools, such as the Low Back Pain Knowledge Questionnaire (LKQ), underscores the importance of targeted health education in improving outcomes; higher LKQ scores correlate with better self-efficacy and reduced disability, highlighting knowledge as a mediating mechanism between health literacy and functional outcomes ref [7]. Together, these findings support the integration of health literacy assessment and tailored educational interventions into routine LBP care to enhance patient engagement and long-term outcomes.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy, Medication Knowledge, and Pain Management
subsections.content:
Health literacy plays a critical role in shaping patients' understanding of pain medications and their ability to engage in effective pain management. Patients with low health literacy demonstrate significantly poorer knowledge of appropriate analgesic use, including dosing, interactions, and non-pharmacological alternatives, as evidenced by lower scores on medication knowledge assessments in chronic pain populations ref [18]. This deficit extends to an inability to identify reliable sources of clinical guidance or to distinguish between over-the-counter and prescription options for pain relief, increasing the risk of misuse and suboptimal outcomes. Furthermore, limited health literacy is associated with reduced awareness of non-pharmacological pain management strategies, such as physical activity, cognitive-behavioral techniques, and heat/cold therapy, which are essential components of a multimodal approach to low back pain ref [18]. While pain intensity itself may not correlate directly with health literacy levels, the capacity to self-manage pain effectively is substantially compromised in individuals with inadequate health literacy, highlighting the need for tailored educational interventions that address both medication literacy and broader pain self-management skills.

Emerging evidence suggests that integrating health literacy-sensitive communication strategies into clinical practice can improve medication adherence and reduce reliance on high-risk analgesics among patients with low back pain. Interventions that use visual aids, simplified language, and teach-back methods have shown promise in enhancing medication knowledge and empowering patients to make informed decisions about their pain care.

Fear-avoidance beliefs (FABs) significantly influence the progression and chronicity of low back pain (LBP), and emerging evidence suggests that health literacy plays a critical role in shaping these cognitive-behavioral responses. Individuals with limited health literacy may misinterpret pain signals, lack understanding of the biopsychosocial nature of LBP, and consequently adopt maladaptive avoidance behaviors, exacerbating disability. A study by Al-Eisa et al. found that women with chronic LBP and inadequate health literacy exhibited significantly higher fear-avoidance beliefs compared to those with adequate literacy, highlighting a direct association between health information processing capacity and psychological responses to pain ref [16].

Health literacy enables patients to critically evaluate health messages, understand therapeutic recommendations, and challenge misconceptions about rest and activity, thereby mitigating fear-driven avoidance. Patients with higher health literacy are more likely to engage in graded activity and perceive pain as manageable rather than threatening, which reduces the reinforcement of avoidance cycles. This relationship underscores the need for tailored health communication strategies that account for literacy levels when delivering pain education and cognitive-behavioral interventions.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy and Patient Empowerment in LBP Self-Management
subsections.content:
Health literacy and patient empowerment are often conflated in discussions of chronic low back pain (LBP) self-management, yet emerging evidence suggests they represent distinct yet interrelated constructs. Camerini and Schulz (2015) argue that health literacy—encompassing the ability to access, understand, and apply health information—must be differentiated from patient empowerment, which involves the capacity to take control of one’s health decisions and actions. Their typology of patients with chronic LBP reveals that high health literacy does not automatically translate to empowerment; some individuals possess adequate knowledge but lack confidence or agency to act, while others with limited literacy demonstrate strong self-efficacy through social support or experiential learning ref [19]. This distinction is critical for designing targeted interventions that address not only information deficits but also psychological and structural barriers to self-management.

Empowerment in LBP self-management is further influenced by patient-provider communication, health system accessibility, and perceived autonomy. Patients with higher empowerment levels are more likely to engage in active coping strategies, adhere to exercise regimens, and seek timely care, independent of their health literacy scores ref [19]. Interventions that foster shared decision-making, provide personalized goal-setting tools, and validate patient experiences may enhance empowerment even among those with low health literacy, suggesting that empowerment can be cultivated beyond cognitive skills. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs to disentangle causal pathways and identify modifiable factors that bridge literacy and empowerment in diverse LBP populations.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy and Healthcare Utilization Outcomes
subsections.content:
Low health literacy is consistently associated with increased healthcare utilization among patients with low back pain (LBP), including higher rates of emergency department visits, specialist referrals, and imaging studies. Patients with inadequate health literacy are less likely to understand appropriate self-management strategies, leading to overreliance on acute care services rather than preventive or conservative interventions. A study by Glassman et al. found that individuals with lumbar degenerative disease and low health literacy had significantly higher resource utilization, including more frequent outpatient visits and diagnostic imaging, independent of disease severity or comorbidities ref [20]. Similarly, MacLeod et al. demonstrated that older adults with inadequate health literacy exhibited higher healthcare expenditures and utilization patterns, including increased hospitalizations and provider visits, even after adjusting for age, comorbidity burden, and socioeconomic status ref [21]. These patterns suggest that health literacy deficits may contribute to inefficient care pathways, where patients seek high-cost interventions due to misunderstanding of condition prognosis or treatment options.

Furthermore, limited health literacy may impair patients’ ability to navigate complex healthcare systems, resulting in delayed or inappropriate care-seeking behaviors. This can manifest as repeated, non-urgent visits or unnecessary procedures driven by misperceptions of pain severity or treatment efficacy. Interventions targeting health literacy, such as simplified patient education materials and decision aids, have shown potential to reduce avoidable utilization, though implementation in LBP populations remains underexplored.

Emerging evidence suggests a significant inverse relationship between health literacy (HL) and pain intensity in patients with chronic low back pain (LBP). Individuals with lower HL consistently report higher pain intensity, as measured by Visual Analogue Scales (VAS), with one study demonstrating a statistically significant correlation (r = -0.270, p = 0.003) among chronic pain patients, independent of age and sex but attenuated after adjusting for education level ref [15]. This association may be mediated by reduced capacity to understand pain mechanisms, adhere to treatment plans, or engage in self-management strategies that mitigate pain perception. Furthermore, lower HL is linked to distorted pain perception, as indicated by elevated scores on the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), suggesting that limited health literacy may impair the cognitive appraisal of pain signals and emotional responses to discomfort ref [15].

Beyond mere symptom reporting, health literacy influences how patients interpret, communicate, and respond to pain, potentially affecting help-seeking behaviors and treatment expectations. Patients with inadequate HL may misattribute pain causes, underestimate the role of non-pharmacological interventions, or over-rely on analgesics, thereby exacerbating pain perception over time. These patterns underscore the need for tailored health communication strategies that enhance HL to improve pain self-regulation and reduce the subjective burden of chronic LBP.

subsections.subsection_title: Core Outcomes and Measurement Standardization in LBP Research
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity in outcome reporting across clinical trials in non-specific low back pain (NSLBP) has long impeded evidence synthesis and clinical decision-making. To address this, the Core Outcome Set in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) initiative and the OMERACT Filter 2.0 framework were instrumental in establishing a standardized core outcome set (COS) for NSLBP research. Ref [1] identified a minimum set of core domains—including pain intensity, physical functioning, health-related quality of life, and patient global impression of change—that should be consistently measured and reported in all clinical trials. This foundational work was further refined by Ref [2], which systematically evaluated and recommended validated measurement instruments for each core domain, ensuring reliability, responsiveness, and clinical relevance. The adoption of these standardized domains and instruments has improved comparability across studies and strengthened the validity of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Despite progress, variability in instrument selection and incomplete reporting persist, particularly in trials involving diverse populations or non-pharmacological interventions, highlighting the need for continued adherence and implementation support.

Standardization efforts have also revealed gaps in the inclusion of patient-centered outcomes such as emotional well-being and return to work, prompting calls for broader domain expansion. Ongoing initiatives aim to integrate patient perspectives more systematically into COS development, ensuring that measurement tools reflect the lived experience of individuals with LBP. Future research must prioritize harmonizing these standards across global settings and validating instruments in low-health-literacy populations to enhance equity in outcome assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Demographic Disparities in Low Back Pain
subsections.content:
The epidemiology of low back pain (LBP) reveals significant global disparities in prevalence, disability, and demographic patterns. In high-income settings, chronic impairing LBP has risen markedly over recent decades, with one study in North Carolina reporting a more than twofold increase in prevalence from 3.9% in 1992 to 10.2% in 2006 across all age groups and racial subgroups, despite stable symptom severity and health care utilization patterns ref [23]. These trends underscore a growing public health burden driven by aging populations and lifestyle factors. In contrast, epidemiological data from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) reveal distinct patterns, with urban populations and occupational groups in enclosed workshops showing higher prevalence than rural laborers, challenging assumptions that physical labor alone drives LBP burden ref [25]. Among older adults in LMICs, LBP is strongly associated with disability and modifiable risk factors such as obesity, sedentary behavior, and poor mental health, as identified in the WHO SAGE study ref [24].

Notably, LBP prevalence and impact vary not only by income level but also by gender, age, and socioeconomic status, with women and older adults consistently reporting higher rates of chronicity and functional limitation. The underrepresentation of LMIC populations in global LBP research has historically skewed understanding, yet emerging evidence highlights that structural factors—including limited access to care, occupational demands, and social determinants—shape disparities beyond mere physical exertion. These findings call for context-specific prevention and management strategies that account for demographic and geographic heterogeneity in LBP burden.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy, Empowerment, and Patient Engagement in LBP
subsections.content:
Health literacy and patient empowerment are distinct yet interrelated constructs that significantly influence patient engagement in low back pain (LBP) management. While health literacy encompasses the cognitive and social skills needed to access, understand, and apply health information, empowerment reflects a patient’s sense of agency and confidence in managing their condition. Ref [2] argues that these concepts, often conflated, must be differentiated to better understand how patients with varying levels of literacy and empowerment engage in self-care. Patients with high health literacy but low empowerment may comprehend medical advice yet fail to act on it, whereas empowered patients with limited literacy may seek support and advocate for themselves effectively. This distinction is critical for tailoring interventions that address both informational and motivational barriers in LBP care.

The development of targeted instruments, such as the HELP questionnaire, underscores the need for validated tools to assess health education literacy specifically in chronic musculoskeletal conditions like LBP. Ref [3] demonstrates that while many patients report moderate to high self-perceived literacy, a substantial proportion (20–30%) struggle with comprehending and applying health education content, highlighting gaps in communication that hinder engagement. Furthermore, health literacy empowers individuals to function effectively as healthcare consumers, enabling informed decision-making and proactive self-management, as outlined in ref [26]. Enhancing patient engagement in LBP thus requires not only improving health literacy but also fostering autonomy, shared decision-making, and supportive clinical environments that validate patient experiences and promote active participation.

subsections.subsection_title: Health Literacy and Its Impact on Low Back Pain Management
subsections.content:
Health literacy significantly influences the management of low back pain (LBP) by shaping patients' ability to access, comprehend, and apply health information to make informed decisions. Patients with low health literacy are more likely to misunderstand treatment instructions, underutilize non-pharmacological interventions, and exhibit poor adherence to self-management strategies, leading to suboptimal clinical outcomes. A systematic review by Edward et al. (ref [27]) found that low health literacy is consistently associated with delayed care-seeking, increased reliance on passive treatments, and reduced engagement in physical activity—key components of effective LBP management. Furthermore, limited health literacy impairs medication knowledge, with patients struggling to identify appropriate analgesics or recognize risks of overuse, as demonstrated in a study by Devraj et al. (ref [15]).

Beyond medication, health literacy affects patients' beliefs and attitudes toward pain and recovery. Briggs et al. (ref [14]) reported that individuals with chronic LBP exhibit significantly lower scores in 'patient attitudes towards their health,' suggesting diminished self-efficacy and agency in managing their condition. Similarly, health literacy is linked to pain perception and intensity; Köppen et al. (ref [6]) found that lower health literacy correlated with higher pain intensity, though this association was attenuated after adjusting for education, indicating a complex interplay between literacy, socioeconomic factors, and pain outcomes. Qualitative insights from Briggs et al. (ref [13]) further reveal that patients with low health literacy often misinterpret LBP as a sign of structural damage, reinforcing fear-avoidance behaviors and hindering rehabilitation.

This scoping review confirms that health literacy significantly influences health outcomes in patients with low back pain, particularly in treatment adherence, self-management, and functional recovery. Patients with limited health literacy exhibit poorer understanding of pain mechanisms and therapeutic interventions, which undermines their ability to engage in evidence-based self-care practices. The integration of health literacy assessments into routine clinical workflows is therefore critical to personalize care and reduce disparities in outcomes, especially in underserved populations.

Supplementary materials should include validated, culturally adapted tools for assessing health literacy in low back pain contexts, such as the Health LiTT instrument, which offers a reliable, technology-enhanced approach to measuring literacy beyond traditional screening tools ref [12]. Additionally, patient education materials must be designed using plain language principles and visual aids to accommodate varying literacy levels, aligning with recommendations for accessible health communication ref [11]. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that link health literacy interventions to objective clinical outcomes, including disability reduction and healthcare utilization patterns ref [22].

subsections.subsection_title: • Pain • Disability • Behaviour • Knowledge and Beliefs • Resource Utilisation
subsections.content:
Pain intensity and disability in low back pain are significantly influenced by patients' knowledge and beliefs regarding their condition. Misconceptions about the nature of back pain, such as the belief that pain equates to tissue damage, are associated with increased disability and maladaptive behaviors, including fear avoidance and activity restriction ref [21]. Patients with limited health literacy often hold more negative illness perceptions, which correlate with higher pain catastrophizing and reduced self-efficacy in managing symptoms ref [24]. Furthermore, inadequate understanding of the biopsychosocial model of pain can lead to overreliance on passive treatments and underutilization of evidence-based strategies such as physical activity and cognitive-behavioral approaches ref [21].

Knowledge gaps also affect help-seeking behavior and resource utilization; patients with lower pain-related knowledge are more likely to seek unnecessary imaging or specialist referrals, contributing to increased healthcare costs without improved outcomes ref [23]. Interventions that improve pain literacy—such as structured education on pain mechanisms and prognosis—have been shown to reduce disability and promote active coping, underscoring the need for tailored health communication ref [21].
